text: Given an integer array nums of length n, build an array ans of length two n, where ans at i equals nums at i, and ans at i plus n also equals nums at i. Return ans.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — this is just nums concatenated with a copy of itself, so one, two, one becomes one, two, one, one, two, one. Am I free to mutate the input, or should I leave it untouched and return a new array? And are there any constraints on the input size?
Either is fine. The array has at most a thousand elements. Let's see a clean solution.

Got it. At most a thousand elements, so one linear pass is plenty. Let me run through the example. One, two, one gives a front half of one, two, one, and a back half of another one, two, one. So the result is one, two, one, one, two, one, and the length doubles to six.

This problem reminds me of direct index mapping. The output is defined position by position, so there's nothing to search — it's a single linear pass. I'll pre-size a fresh array of length two n and fill each index straight from its definition: ans at i and ans at i plus n both get nums at i. That reads right off the spec, and it sidesteps the one gotcha this problem has.

If instead you append to nums in place, you must freeze the length first — int n equals nums dot size — and loop while i is less than n. If you carelessly loop while i is less than nums dot size, every push back grows the size, so i never catches the moving bound. That's an infinite loop that grows the vector until you run out of memory. Freezing n cuts that chase.

Here's the plan. One: freeze n as the original size. Two: make an array of size two n. Three: for each i below n, write nums at i into both ans at i and ans at i plus n, then return ans. It's index assignment on a pre-sized array — no push back, no length-chasing, and linear time. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Code it — and show the in-place version too.

Alright, let me code this up. The fresh-array version is the clearest: allocate two n slots, then one loop fills the front half and the back half with plain index assignment. The in-place variant freezes n, then appends nums at i, so it reads the front half and writes the back half. One thing worth flagging — the easy line to get wrong is the in-place loop bound. It must be i less than the frozen n, never nums dot size, or the loop chases its own growth forever. Both are linear time. The in-place one uses no extra container; the fresh one is easier to reason about.
In the in-place version you read nums at i while pushing to the same vector. Is that safe?

Yes, for two reasons. First, i stays below n, so I only ever read the front half, zero up to n, while push back writes from n up to two n. Those regions are disjoint, so a freshly appended element is never re-read. Second, I index nums at i fresh on every iteration, so nothing stale survives a reallocation, and push back is required to work even when its argument lives in the same vector. The one thing I'd avoid is caching a reference, int ampersand r equals nums at i, across the push — reallocation would invalidate r. Reserving two n up front also guarantees no reallocation happens at all.

Let's dry-run the code. One, three, two, one, so n is four, and I expect one, three, two, one, one, three, two, one. The row that matters is the last, i equals three: it fills ans at three and ans at seven, the final slot, and then i reaches n and the loop stops — exactly n iterations. Every i satisfies ans at i equals ans at i plus n equals nums at i, so that matches. Corner case: n equal to one turns x into x, x, with no special handling.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear. Extra space is constant for the in-place version, or linear for the output either way. Oh, one more thing — if I only needed to query the concatenation rather than materialize it, I wouldn't build anything: ans at i is just nums at i mod n, which is constant space. That same i mod n trick is how duplicating the array shows up as preprocessing in circular-array problems — doubling the array turns a wrap-around range into a plain linear one.
Good. You picked the clearest version, knew the infinite-loop trap cold, and reasoned carefully about read-while-writing safety and reallocation. Nice clean pass on a warm-up.
